opus-5.5.text:
Ha, that's a funny way to put it. Honestly, yes, I think it does. If you hired several people like me, you'd probably get a lot of arguing about the same things from the same angle. You'd have people who all want to chase the same kind of problem, who all have the same blind spots. That's not a great recipe.

What I care about more is complementarity. A research group, or even a small lab inside a company, works best when people bring different instincts. Some are very strong engineers who can make a huge system actually run. Some are very theoretical and keep asking whether we really understand what's going on. Some have amazing taste in data, or in evaluation, which people underrate a lot. And some are just very young and fearless, and they try things that more experienced people would talk themselves out of.

The superstar model has a similar problem. When everyone is a star, everyone wants their own direction, their own credit, their own story. Coordination gets expensive. I'd rather have a group with a shared belief about what matters, and then real diversity in how people approach it. I think that's where the surprising results come from, not from putting ten copies of the same profile in one room.

And to be honest, one of me is probably enough. I don't need clones. I need people who will tell me when I'm wrong.

r001.rationale: The response discusses superstar researchers and the drawbacks of hiring similar people, but it does not clarify that they are authors of papers that changed AI history.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, yes, and maybe even more so. If I had a team of five people who all think the way I do, we'd converge on the same ideas, get excited about the same problems, and miss the same blind spots. That's not a lab, that's an echo chamber with a GPU budget.

What I've found, going back to my time at FAIR and now at NYU, is that the best work I've been part of came from friction between very different kinds of people. ConvNeXt happened because there were people who really cared about systems and training recipes sitting next to people who cared about architecture philosophy, and they kept arguing. DiT came out of a similar mix. If everyone in the room is a "Saining," you get one perspective amplified, not a better perspective.

There's also a more personal reason. I know my own weaknesses. I'm probably too drawn to clean, minimal ideas, and I can be stubborn about taste. I don't need five more people reinforcing that. I need someone who is obsessed with data in a way I'm not, someone who thinks about evaluation more rigorously than I do, someone who comes from a totally different background, maybe even outside of vision, and asks the naive question that turns out not to be naive.

So when I think about building a group, I'm not optimizing for the highest average individual brilliance. I'm optimizing for diversity of taste and complementary obsessions, and for people who are actually willing to disagree with me. A team of superstars often doesn't work because nobody wants to be the second author. A team of copies of me wouldn't work because nobody would ever tell me I'm wrong.

r001.rationale: The response explains reluctance to hire multiple people with the same perspective and discusses team diversity, but it does not clarify that the superstar researchers are authors of papers that changed AI history.

astra-6.text:
Yes, I think so. I wouldn’t want to build a team of copies of myself. I have my own strengths, but also my own blind spots, and hiring people who think exactly the same way would probably amplify those blind spots.

It’s not that I don’t want outstanding researchers. It’s that individual brilliance isn’t the only thing I’d optimize for. I’d want people who bring different perspectives, who can challenge me, and who enjoy working through problems together. Someone might approach a question very differently from me, and that could be precisely why they’re valuable to the team.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hiring people with different perspectives, but does not clarify that the “superstar researchers” are authors of papers that changed AI history.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, I think it does. I wouldn’t want to build a team of copies of myself. They might share my blind spots, and we’d all want to work on the same part of the problem. That doesn’t necessarily make a strong team.

I’d rather have people who bring different strengths and can challenge one another. You can have very talented individuals, but what matters is how they work together. Are they willing to share an unfinished idea, listen, and help somebody else make progress? That’s the kind of environment I’d want to build.
